concepts.name: Definition and Scope of an Ecosystem
key_dimensions: Tansley's original definition (1935) vs. modern interpretations — who coined the term and when
Ecosystem as a functional unit vs. structural unit — UPSC often tests this distinction
Smallest vs. largest ecosystem — a drop of water vs. the biosphere (trap: biosphere itself as an ecosystem)
Difference between ecosystem, biome, and biosphere — overlapping terms frequently confused in MCQs

concepts.name: Abiotic Components of an Ecosystem
key_dimensions: Classification: climatic (light, temperature, water), edaphic (soil), and inorganic chemicals
Role of limiting factors (Liebig's Law of Minimum) — which single abiotic factor limits productivity
Difference between abiotic and abiogenic — trap in terminology
How abiotic components differ between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems (e.g., light penetration in aquatic)

concepts.name: Biotic Components: Producers, Consumers, and Decomposers
key_dimensions: Autotrophs vs. heterotrophs — chemoautotrophs as producers (trap: not all producers use sunlight)
Classification of consumers: primary, secondary, tertiary, and omnivores — where do omnivores fit in trophic levels
Decomposers vs. detritivores vs. saprotrophs — distinctions UPSC exploits in traps
Role of detritivores in nutrient cycling vs. energy flow — which do they primarily drive

concepts.name: Trophic Levels and Energy Flow
key_dimensions: 10% Law (Lindeman's Law) — energy transfer efficiency and its implications for food chain length
Why food chains are typically limited to 4–5 trophic levels — thermodynamic reasoning
Difference between food chain and food web — which is more realistic and why
Grazing food chain (GFC) vs. Detritus food chain (DFC) — which dominates in forests vs. open oceans (trap)

concepts.name: Ecological Pyramids: Numbers, Biomass, and Energy
key_dimensions: Inverted pyramids: pyramid of numbers (parasitic chain) and pyramid of biomass (aquatic ecosystems) — which can NEVER be inverted
Pyramid of energy is always upright — the one exception that is not an exception (UPSC trap)
Difference between standing crop and standing state — standing state includes inorganic nutrients
Limitations of ecological pyramids — do not account for saprophytes, omnivores, or seasonal changes

concepts.name: Food Chains: Grazing vs. Detritus
key_dimensions: Starting point: GFC starts with living plants; DFC starts with dead organic matter (detritus)
Which food chain contributes more to energy flow in terrestrial ecosystems — DFC dominates in forests
Interconnection between GFC and DFC — how they feed into each other
Role of DFC in nutrient cycling vs. energy dissipation

concepts.name: Productivity: Primary and Secondary
key_dimensions: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) vs. Net Primary Productivity (NPP) — NPP = GPP minus respiration loss
Net Primary Productivity vs. Net Ecosystem Productivity — trap: NEP accounts for heterotrophic respiration too
Highest NPP ecosystems: tropical rainforests and estuaries vs. lowest: deserts and deep oceans
Secondary productivity — defined only for heterotrophs; there is no gross/net distinction commonly tested

concepts.name: Biogeochemical Cycles: Gaseous vs. Sedimentary
key_dimensions: Gaseous cycles (carbon, nitrogen, oxygen) vs. sedimentary cycles (phosphorus, sulfur) — reservoir difference
Phosphorus cycle has no atmospheric phase — making it a 'perfect' sedimentary cycle and a slow cycle
Which cycles are most affected by human activity — carbon and nitrogen cycles (eutrophication, climate change)
Reservoir vs. exchange pool in nutrient cycles — trap: atmosphere is the reservoir for gaseous cycles

concepts.name: Carbon Cycle and Ecosystem Carbon Budget
key_dimensions: Biological processes (photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition) vs. geological processes (weathering, volcanism)
Role of oceans as carbon sinks vs. carbon sources — when does the ocean become a source
Peat bogs and permafrost as carbon stores — relevance to climate feedback loops
Human interventions: fossil fuel combustion, deforestation — net effect on atmospheric CO₂

concepts.name: Nitrogen Cycle: Fixation, Nitrification, Denitrification
key_dimensions: Nitrogen fixation pathways: biological (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria) vs. industrial (Haber process) vs. atmospheric (lightning)
Nitrification vs. Denitrification — which adds and which removes nitrogen from the soil
Ammonification — the role of decomposers in regenerating ammonium from organic nitrogen
Trap: Rhizobium is symbiotic (legumes), Azotobacter is free-living — UPSC frequently mixes these

concepts.name: Types of Ecosystems: Natural vs. Artificial
key_dimensions: Natural (forest, grassland, desert, aquatic) vs. artificial/man-made (crop fields, aquaria, urban ecosystems)
Self-sustaining vs. non-self-sustaining ecosystems — artificial ecosystems need external energy inputs
Stability of natural vs. artificial ecosystems — monoculture agriculture as least stable
Crop ecosystem as a special case — subsidized energy through human labor and inputs

concepts.name: Aquatic Ecosystems: Lentic vs. Lotic
key_dimensions: Lentic (standing water: lakes, ponds, swamps) vs. lotic (flowing water: rivers, streams) — structural differences
Zonation in lakes: littoral, limnetic, profundal, and benthic zones — which zone has no photosynthesis
Thermal stratification in lakes: epilimnion, thermocline, hypolimnion — and seasonal overturn
Oligotrophic vs. eutrophic lakes — succession from oligotrophic to eutrophic (trap: eutrophication is natural AND anthropogenic)

concepts.name: Terrestrial Ecosystems: Forest, Grassland, and Desert
key_dimensions: Basis of classification: rainfall and temperature — biome boundaries defined by climate
Net primary productivity ranking: tropical forest > temperate forest > boreal forest > grassland > desert
Grassland types: tropical (savanna) vs. temperate (steppes, prairies) — dominant fauna differences
Desert ecosystem adaptations — xerophytes and the concept of C4 and CAM photosynthesis as adaptation

concepts.name: Estuaries and Wetland Ecosystems
key_dimensions: Estuary as a transition zone — ecotone between marine and freshwater, highest biodiversity and productivity
Wetlands as 'kidneys of the earth' — functions: water purification, flood control, carbon sequestration
Ramsar Convention and its definition of wetlands — broader than commonly understood (includes coral reefs, mangroves)
Mangroves as a special wetland type — differences from other wetlands in terms of salinity tolerance and carbon storage (blue carbon)

concepts.name: Ecotone and Edge Effect
key_dimensions: Definition of ecotone — transitional zone between two ecosystems, e.g., mangrove between land and sea
Edge effect — higher species diversity and density at ecotones than in either adjacent ecosystem
Examples of ecotones: mangroves, estuary, grassland-forest boundary — UPSC uses these as trap examples
Ecotone vs. ecocline — ecotone is a sharp boundary, ecocline is a gradual gradient

concepts.name: Ecological Succession: Primary and Secondary
key_dimensions: Primary succession (bare rock, new volcanic island) vs. secondary succession (abandoned farmland, burned forest) — key difference is presence of soil
Seral stages and climax community — hydrosere (aquatic to terrestrial) vs. xerosere (dry to mesic)
Pioneer species in primary succession: lichens (on rock) vs. grasses (on land) — which is the first colonizer
Convergence: different seral communities converging to the same climax — concept of climatic climax vs. edaphic climax

concepts.name: Homeostasis and Stability in Ecosystems
key_dimensions: Resistance vs. resilience — resistance is ability to resist disturbance; resilience is ability to recover after disturbance
Species diversity and ecosystem stability — more diverse ecosystems are generally more stable (but exceptions exist)
Positive vs. negative feedback mechanisms — which destabilizes and which stabilizes an ecosystem
Concept of ecological balance — how keystone species maintain ecosystem homeostasis

concepts.name: Decomposition Process and Its Regulation
key_dimensions: Steps of decomposition: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralization — sequence matters
Humification vs. mineralization — humification produces humus (slow decomposition); mineralization releases inorganic nutrients
Factors affecting decomposition rate: temperature, moisture, oxygen, and chemical quality of detritus (lignin and chitin slow it)
Why decomposition is slower in waterlogged/anaerobic conditions — leads to peat formation (carbon sequestration trap)

concepts.name: Keystone Species and Their Ecosystem Role
key_dimensions: Definition: species with disproportionately large effect relative to their biomass — different from dominant species
Examples: sea otters (kelp forest), elephants (savanna), tigers (trophic cascade) — UPSC uses these for application questions
Keystone species vs. umbrella species vs. flagship species — distinctions frequently confused
Trophic cascade effect — removal of a keystone predator causes cascading changes through the food web

concepts.name: Energy Budget and Assimilation Efficiency in Ecosystems
key_dimensions: Assimilation efficiency vs. ecological efficiency vs. production efficiency — three different measures of energy use
Net production efficiency = net production / assimilation — higher in ectotherms than endotherms (trap: why warm-blooded animals are less efficient)
Trophic level transfer efficiency (TLTE) — typically 5–20%, not always exactly 10%
Implications for human diet: eating lower on the food chain supports more people — policy relevance for UPSC Mains
